h1: Stopping a boil-over and keeping it from happening again
title: Stopping a Boil-Over on Brew Day | Craft Beer School
desc: Why wort boils over at the hot break, how to stop it in seconds and how kettle size, heat control and antifoam keep it from happening again.
teaser: Wort foams up at the start of the boil. Here is how to stop it spilling and what to do differently next time.
standfirst: A boil-over leaves sticky wort on the stove, the floor and sometimes the gas burner. It almost always happens in the first few minutes of the boil. Here is why, how to stop one fast and how to prevent the next.
sections:
Wort is full of proteins from the malt. As it approaches the boil, those proteins start to clump and rise in a thick foam called the hot break. The foam traps steam and grows quickly. In a full kettle it climbs over the rim in seconds.

The danger window is short: from the first bubbles to a few minutes into a rolling boil. Once the hot break has formed and the foam collapses, the risk drops a lot. The other common trigger is the first hop addition. Pellets dropped into near-boiling wort give the bubbles somewhere to form and the foam surges. Our guide on what happens during the boil explains the chemistry.
How to stop one in seconds

• Cut the heat. Turn the burner right down or off. On gas, this works within seconds.
  • Spray the foam. A spray bottle of clean water misted over the surface knocks the foam down.
  • Stir. A long spoon breaks the foam and releases trapped steam.
  • Blow across it. It sounds daft. It works on a small kettle.

Keep the spray bottle by the kettle from the start of the heat-up. When the foam starts climbing, you have no time to fetch it.

Electric all-in-one systems react more slowly than gas. Their elements stay hot for a while after switching off. On those systems, turn the power down earlier, while the wort is still a few degrees below boiling, rather than waiting for the foam to appear.

On a domestic LPG stove, a boil-over is more than a mess. Wort pouring down the sides can put out the burner flame while gas keeps flowing. Many domestic stoves have no flame failure device to cut the gas.

If the flame goes out, turn off the gas at the knob straight away. Do not relight until the burner is wiped dry and any gas smell has cleared. Keep the room ventilated during the boil. Sticky wort that bakes into burner ports also gives a poor, yellow flame next time. Clean them with a pin once the stove is cold. Our guide to homebrew safety covers the wider risks.

The most reliable prevention is room. Aim to fill the kettle no more than about three quarters full at the start of the boil. A 20 litre batch with a 26 litre pre-boil volume wants a kettle of about 35 litres or more.

If your kettle is too small, split the boil across two pots or reduce the batch size. A boil-over in a brimming kettle cannot be stopped fast enough. Our guide to choosing a kettle size has the volumes worked out.
Control the heat at the break

Most boil-overs come from full heat applied right through the hot break. Bring the wort up at full power, then turn the heat down just before it reaches a boil. Let the hot break form gently. Once the foam has risen and fallen, turn the heat back up to a steady rolling boil.

Wait to add the first hops until the hot break has passed. Most recipes allow for this. A 60 minute addition that goes in five minutes after the boil starts barely changes bitterness. It removes the most common trigger for a sudden surge.

Food-grade silicone antifoam, sold to homebrewers in small dropper bottles, reduces foaming in both the kettle and the fermenter. A few drops per batch, as the label specifies, is enough. Most of it settles out with the trub and yeast.

Some brewers drop a few sanitised stainless marbles into the kettle to give steady, small bubbles. Others swear by a lid half on. We prefer headspace and heat control because they always work. Understanding what the hot break does for the beer, beyond the mess it makes, is part of the boil science we cover in our fundamentals course.
Set up your stove before the next brew

Before your next brew day, measure your kettle and mark the three-quarters line inside with a strip of tape on the handle or a notch on your dip stick. Fill a spray bottle with water and put it on the counter next to the stove. On the day, turn the heat down as the first bubbles appear and stay at the kettle until the foam has fallen.
faqs: When is wort most likely to boil over?
During the hot break, from the first bubbles to a few minutes into the boil. The first hop addition is the other common moment.
How full should my kettle be?
No more than about three quarters full at the start of the boil.
What should I do if a boil-over puts out my gas flame?
Turn off the gas at the knob immediately. Do not relight until the burner is dry and any gas smell has cleared.
